concepts.name: Variables and data types
concepts.definition: Storing values in variables and using a language's built-in and composite data types (numbers, text, records, structures).

concepts.name: Control structures
concepts.definition: Conditionals and loops that decide which statements run and how often.

concepts.name: Functions and procedures
concepts.definition: Defining and calling named, parameterized pieces of code (functions, methods, procedures, subroutines).
concepts.notes: Mathematical "functions" (discrete math) are tagged sets-relations-functions instead.

concepts.name: Recursion
concepts.definition: Functions or definitions that refer to themselves, solving a problem through smaller instances of the same problem.

concepts.name: Arrays and strings
concepts.definition: Indexed sequences of values and text strings, and the basic operations on them.

concepts.name: File input and output
concepts.definition: Reading and writing files and other input/output streams from a program.
synonyms: reading/writing data and objects from/to files
concepts.notes: Operating-system file systems are a separate concept (file-systems).

phrases: reading/writing data and objects from/to files

concepts.name: Exceptions and error handling
concepts.definition: Detecting, signaling, and recovering from errors at run time.

concepts.name: Pointers and dynamic memory
concepts.definition: Addresses, pointers, and allocating and freeing memory at run time, including avoiding leaks.
concepts.notes: Operating-system memory management is a separate concept (os-memory-management).

concepts.name: Modularity and decomposition
concepts.definition: Breaking a program into separate, independently understandable parts (top-down design, modules).
concepts.first_seen: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities / CSCI 1133

concepts.name: C
concepts.definition: Programming in the C language.
concepts.notes: Languages are listed because the committee may ask which languages schools require.

concepts.name: C++
concepts.definition: Programming in the C++ language.

concepts.name: Java
concepts.definition: Programming in the Java language.

concepts.name: Python
concepts.definition: Programming in the Python language.

concepts.name: Object-oriented programming
concepts.definition: Organizing programs around classes and objects that bundle data with the operations on it.

concepts.name: Inheritance and polymorphism
concepts.definition: Defining classes in terms of other classes and writing code that works across related types.
concepts.notes: Parametric polymorphism (generics) is tagged generics instead.

concepts.name: Encapsulation and interfaces
concepts.definition: Hiding a component's internals behind a defined interface that clients program against.

concepts.name: Object-oriented design
concepts.definition: Deciding which classes a system needs and how they relate, before or while writing them.

concepts.name: Design patterns
concepts.definition: Reusable, named solutions to recurring software design problems.

concepts.name: Generics and templates
concepts.definition: Writing code once for many element types (templates, generics, parametric polymorphism).

concepts.name: Specifications and contracts
concepts.definition: Stating precisely what a component must do (preconditions, postconditions, specifications) separately from how.

concepts.name: GUIs and event-driven programming
concepts.definition: Building graphical user interfaces and programs that respond to user and system events.

concepts.name: Web and client-server applications
concepts.definition: Building applications split between clients and servers, including web applications.

concepts.name: Code quality and style
concepts.definition: Writing readable, maintainable code: consistent style, documentation, coding standards.

concepts.name: Software testing
concepts.definition: Checking that code behaves as intended by writing and running tests.

concepts.name: Test-driven development
concepts.definition: Writing tests before the code they check, and using them to drive the design.

concepts.name: Debugging
concepts.definition: Finding and fixing the causes of incorrect program behavior, including with debugging tools.

concepts.name: Version control
concepts.definition: Tracking and sharing changes to code with a version-control system.

concepts.name: Development tools and environments
concepts.definition: The everyday tools of programming beyond the language itself: IDEs, build tools, documentation tools.

concepts.name: Unix and shell scripting
concepts.definition: Working in a Unix environment and automating tasks with shell scripts and Unix tools.

concepts.name: Code review and continuous integration
concepts.definition: Team practices for checking and integrating changes: reviewing each other's code and building/testing automatically.

concepts.name: Software development process
concepts.definition: The stages and models of building software over its life: requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance.

concepts.name: Requirements engineering
concepts.definition: Finding out and writing down what a system must do, and for whom.

concepts.name: Software project management
concepts.definition: Planning, scheduling, and managing risk in a software project.

concepts.name: Team projects
concepts.definition: Students building software together in teams.

concepts.name: Large software project
concepts.definition: A sustained project substantially larger than a typical assignment, usually spanning weeks or the whole term.

concepts.name: Libraries and reusable components
concepts.definition: Building software from existing libraries and components, and designing components for reuse.

concepts.name: Program and algorithm correctness
concepts.definition: Arguing or proving that a program or algorithm does what its specification says (assertions, invariants, correctness proofs, formal methods).

concepts.name: Problem-solving heuristics
concepts.definition: Explicit strategies for attacking unfamiliar problems (working backwards, simplifying, trying cases).
concepts.first_seen: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University / CS 2104
concepts.notes: Kept because VT 2104 makes it a concrete practice; generic "problem solving" elsewhere is not tagged.

concepts.name: Abstract data types
concepts.definition: Defining a data type by its operations rather than its representation, and implementing it behind that interface.

concepts.name: Linked lists
concepts.definition: Sequences built from nodes that point to the next node.
concepts.first_seen: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities / CSCI 1933

concepts.name: Stacks and queues
concepts.definition: Last-in-first-out and first-in-first-out collections.

concepts.name: Trees
concepts.definition: Hierarchical structures of nodes with children, including binary trees and tree traversal.
concepts.first_seen: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities / CSCI 1933
concepts.notes: Graph-theory trees in discrete math are tagged graph-theory instead.

concepts.name: Search trees and balanced trees
concepts.definition: Trees ordered for fast lookup, and the balancing schemes that keep them shallow.

concepts.name: Heaps and priority queues
concepts.definition: Collections that always give back the smallest (or largest) item first, usually implemented as heaps.
concepts.first_seen: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities / CSCI 4041

concepts.name: Hash tables
concepts.definition: Storing and finding keys by hashing them into an array of buckets.

concepts.name: Graph data structures
concepts.definition: Representing graphs in a program, e.g. with adjacency lists or matrices.
concepts.first_seen: The Pennsylvania State University (University Park) / CMPSC 222
concepts.notes: Graphs as mathematics are graph-theory; graph algorithms are graph-algorithms.

concepts.name: Asymptotic analysis
concepts.definition: Describing how an algorithm's running time or memory grows with input size (big-O and related notation).
synonyms: analysis of time and space requirements

phrases: analysis of time and space requirements

concepts.name: Recurrence relations
concepts.definition: Equations that define a sequence or running time in terms of smaller inputs, and solving them.

concepts.name: Sorting
concepts.definition: Algorithms that put items in order and their trade-offs.

concepts.name: Searching
concepts.definition: Algorithms for finding an item in a collection (e.g. linear and binary search).
concepts.notes: Graph search is graph-algorithms; AI search is state-space-search.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer
concepts.definition: Solving a problem by splitting it into smaller subproblems, solving them, and combining the results.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming
concepts.definition: Solving problems by building up and reusing solutions to overlapping subproblems.

concepts.name: Greedy algorithms
concepts.definition: Algorithms that build a solution by repeatedly taking the locally best choice.
concepts.first_seen: The University of Texas at Austin / C S 331

concepts.name: Graph algorithms
concepts.definition: Algorithms on graphs such as traversal (BFS/DFS), shortest paths, and minimum spanning trees.

concepts.name: String matching
concepts.definition: Finding occurrences of a pattern in a text efficiently.

concepts.name: Randomized algorithms
concepts.definition: Algorithms that use random choices, and analyzing their expected behavior.

concepts.name: Parallel algorithms
concepts.definition: Designing and analyzing algorithms whose steps can run at the same time.

concepts.name: Approximation and intractability
concepts.definition: Coping with hard problems by finding provably near-optimal answers or other workarounds.
concepts.first_seen: The University of Texas at Austin / C S 331

concepts.name: Backtracking
concepts.definition: Exploring a space of partial solutions and undoing choices that can't succeed.

concepts.name: Lower bounds
concepts.definition: Proving that no algorithm can solve a problem faster than some limit.

concepts.name: Finite automata and regular languages
concepts.definition: Machines with finitely many states, and the regular languages and expressions they recognize.

concepts.name: Context-free grammars and pushdown automata
concepts.definition: Grammars that generate nested structures, the pushdown automata that recognize them, and the Chomsky hierarchy.

concepts.name: Turing machines
concepts.definition: The standard formal model of a general-purpose computer.

concepts.name: Computability and undecidability
concepts.definition: Which problems no algorithm can solve, such as the halting problem.

concepts.name: NP-completeness and complexity classes
concepts.definition: Classifying problems by the resources needed to solve them (P, NP, NP-complete) and reductions between them.

concepts.name: Propositional logic
concepts.definition: Logic of true/false statements joined by and, or, not, and implies; truth tables.

concepts.name: Predicate logic
concepts.definition: Logic with predicates and quantifiers (for all, there exists), also called first-order logic.

concepts.name: Proof techniques
concepts.definition: Methods of mathematical proof (direct, contradiction, cases) and writing rigorous arguments.

concepts.name: Mathematical induction
concepts.definition: Proving statements for all natural numbers or all structures by a base case and an inductive step.

concepts.name: Sets, relations, and functions
concepts.definition: The basic objects of discrete math: sets, relations and their properties, and functions as mappings.

concepts.name: Counting and combinatorics
concepts.definition: Counting the size of sets and arrangements (permutations, combinations).

concepts.name: Graph theory
concepts.definition: Graphs and trees as mathematical objects, and their properties.

concepts.name: Boolean algebra
concepts.definition: Algebra of true/false values, used in logic and in circuit design.

concepts.name: Number theory and modular arithmetic
concepts.definition: Integers, divisibility, and arithmetic modulo n.

concepts.name: Game theory
concepts.definition: Mathematical models of strategic decisions among competing players.

concepts.name: Probability
concepts.definition: Random events and variables, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, and expectation.

concepts.name: Statistics
concepts.definition: Drawing conclusions from data: estimation, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, regression.

concepts.name: Linear algebra
concepts.definition: Vectors, matrices, linear systems, and eigenvalues, and computing with them.

concepts.name: Numerical methods
concepts.definition: Computing approximate answers to continuous math problems with floating-point arithmetic.

concepts.name: Information theory and coding
concepts.definition: Measuring information, compressing data, and codes that detect or correct errors.

concepts.name: Data analysis and visualization
concepts.definition: Exploring real datasets: summarizing, visualizing, and computing results from them.

concepts.name: Database design and the relational model
concepts.definition: Modeling data with entity-relationship diagrams and relational tables.

concepts.name: Database queries
concepts.definition: Querying a database from a program or query language.
concepts.first_seen: The Pennsylvania State University (University Park) / CMPSC 221

concepts.name: Database storage, recovery, and concurrency
concepts.definition: How a database stores data physically and stays correct under failures and concurrent use.

concepts.name: Search in AI
concepts.definition: Solving AI problems by searching a space of states, with uninformed and heuristic (e.g. A*) search.

concepts.name: Game playing and adversarial search
concepts.definition: Choosing moves against an opponent, e.g. minimax with alpha-beta pruning.

concepts.name: Constraint satisfaction
concepts.definition: Finding assignments to variables that satisfy a set of constraints.

concepts.name: Knowledge representation and reasoning
concepts.definition: Representing facts in a formal language and drawing conclusions from them by inference.

concepts.name: Reasoning under uncertainty
concepts.definition: Making inferences and decisions when facts are uncertain, using probability.

concepts.name: Planning and decision making
concepts.definition: Choosing sequences of actions to reach goals.

concepts.name: Machine learning
concepts.definition: Building models from data: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.

concepts.name: Deep learning and generative AI
concepts.definition: Neural networks with many layers, and models that generate text or images.

concepts.name: Data representation and computer arithmetic
concepts.definition: How numbers, characters, and other data are encoded in bits, and arithmetic on those encodings.

concepts.name: Logic gates and combinational circuits
concepts.definition: Building circuits from logic gates whose outputs depend only on current inputs.

concepts.name: Sequential circuits
concepts.definition: Circuits with memory (flip-flops, registers, clocks) whose outputs depend on past inputs.

concepts.name: Assembly and machine language
concepts.definition: Programming directly in a processor's instructions and their textual (assembly) form.

concepts.name: Instruction set architecture
concepts.definition: The instructions, formats, registers, and addressing modes a processor exposes to software.
concepts.first_seen: University of Minnesota, Twin Cities / CSCI 2021

concepts.name: Processor design
concepts.definition: How a CPU is built: datapath, control unit, and arithmetic-logic unit.

concepts.name: Pipelining
concepts.definition: Overlapping the stages of several instructions to speed up a processor, and the hazards this creates.

concepts.name: Memory hierarchy and caches
concepts.definition: Layers of faster, smaller memory (caches) in front of slower, larger memory, and their effect on performance.

concepts.name: I/O and interrupts
concepts.definition: How the processor communicates with devices: buses, polling, interrupts, and DMA.

concepts.name: Hardware parallelism
concepts.definition: Hardware features that run work in parallel, beyond pipelining.

concepts.name: Performance analysis and optimization
concepts.definition: Measuring and improving how fast programs run, often using knowledge of the hardware.

concepts.name: Compiling, linking, and loading
concepts.definition: How source code becomes an executable: compiling, assembling, linking, and loading.

concepts.name: Processes
concepts.definition: Running programs as processes, creating and controlling them, and switching between them.

concepts.name: Threads and concurrency
concepts.definition: Running several threads of control at once and writing concurrent programs.

concepts.name: Synchronization and deadlock
concepts.definition: Coordinating concurrent threads or processes safely (locks, atomic operations) and avoiding deadlock.

concepts.name: CPU scheduling
concepts.definition: How an operating system decides which process or thread runs next.

concepts.name: Memory management
concepts.definition: How memory is allocated to programs, including heap allocation and garbage collection.

concepts.name: Virtual memory and address spaces
concepts.definition: Giving each program its own address space mapped onto physical memory, with page tables.

concepts.name: File systems
concepts.definition: How an operating system organizes and stores files and directories.
synonyms: file system organization and access methods

phrases: file system organization and access methods

concepts.name: Interprocess communication and signals
concepts.definition: Ways processes exchange data and notifications (pipes, signals, shared memory).

concepts.name: System calls and OS interfaces
concepts.definition: How programs request services from the operating system.

concepts.name: Protection and isolation
concepts.definition: Keeping programs from interfering with each other or the OS, through protection modes and access control.

concepts.name: Virtualization
concepts.definition: Running multiple virtual machines or virtualized resources on one physical machine.
concepts.first_seen: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University / CS 3214

concepts.name: Network programming
concepts.definition: Writing programs that communicate over a network, e.g. with sockets.

concepts.name: Network protocols
concepts.definition: The rules by which computers communicate over networks (e.g. TCP/IP, DNS).

concepts.name: Distributed systems
concepts.definition: Systems of cooperating computers, and remote procedure calls between them.

concepts.name: Security fundamentals
concepts.definition: Basic ideas of computer and information security: threats, protections, and secure, robust programs.

concepts.name: Cryptography
concepts.definition: Encrypting and authenticating data, and cryptographic protocols.

concepts.name: Information assurance and incident response
concepts.definition: Organizational side of security: protecting information assets, choosing protection levels, intrusion detection, and responding to incidents.

concepts.name: Programming paradigms
concepts.definition: Comparing major styles of programming (imperative, object-oriented, functional, logic, declarative).

concepts.name: Functional programming
concepts.definition: Programming with pure functions and values, avoiding mutable state.

concepts.name: Logic programming
concepts.definition: Programming by stating facts and rules and letting the system search for answers.

concepts.name: Higher-order functions
concepts.definition: Functions that take or return other functions (lambdas, closures).

concepts.name: Type systems
concepts.definition: How a language classifies values into types and checks programs against them.

concepts.name: Syntax and semantics
concepts.definition: Formally describing what programs in a language look like and what they mean.

concepts.name: Parsing
concepts.definition: Turning program text into a structured form (lexing, parsing).

concepts.name: Compilers and interpreters
concepts.definition: Building programs that translate or execute other programs.

concepts.name: Scope, parameter passing, and run-time organization
concepts.definition: How names are bound, how arguments are passed, and how calls are organized at run time (the call stack).

concepts.name: Ethical principles and reasoning
concepts.definition: Ethical theories and codes, and applying them to decisions in computing.

concepts.name: Professional responsibility
concepts.definition: The duties and conduct expected of computing professionals, including professional codes.

concepts.name: Privacy
concepts.definition: Collection and use of personal data, surveillance, and privacy protection.

concepts.name: Intellectual property
concepts.definition: Copyright, patents, licenses, and open-source software.

concepts.name: Computing law and policy
concepts.definition: Laws and public policy that govern computing.

concepts.name: Social impact of computing
concepts.definition: Effects of computing on society: fairness, inequality, free speech, social media, environment.
concepts.first_seen: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University / CS 3604

concepts.name: History of computing
concepts.definition: How computing and its technologies developed.
concepts.first_seen: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University / CS 3604

concepts.name: Technical communication
concepts.definition: Writing and presenting technical material: reports, documentation, talks, demos.

concepts.name: Career preparation
concepts.definition: Preparing for jobs: career paths, résumés, interviews, and co-op or internship processes.

concepts.name: Overview of computing as a field
concepts.definition: Surveys of what computer science covers, its research, and its application domains.

concepts.name: Academic orientation
concepts.definition: Introducing students to the degree program, its requirements, and campus resources.

rows.title: Introduction to Computer Science
rows.description:
1. Structure of the CS curriculum and program requirements in EECS department, Overview of student groups and extra-curricular activities.
2. What does a programmer do in a typical job and in a typical career? What does it mean to write computer code?
a. Harnessing the power of computers and of large datasets
b. Requires creativity, insights about human needs, knowledge about computers, and knowledge a out application domains.
c. Building abstractions by connecting simpler elements to larger conceptual entities.
d. The enabler role of the computer science discipline.
3. What is a computer program or an App?
a. Life-cycle and examples of Apps and small/large computer programs
b. Courses in the CS curriculum that address various aspects of the program/App life-cycle.
4. Connection of Mathematics, Statistics, Sciences, and other engineering disciplines with a career and education in computer science.
5. Nature of Internet and its relationship to various aspects of computer science and also to various courses in CS curriculum.
6. Application domains and computer science’s impacts in these domains:
a. Everyday business operations
b. Finance and banking
rows.notes: UC's catalog description may be cut off (ends without punctuation).

tags.notes: "Life-cycle and examples of Apps" in an orientation overview.

rows.title: Computer Science 1
rows.description: Introduction to computer science with emphasis upon structured and object-oriented programming, algorithm design, and problem-solving. Currently, C++ is used as the computer language.

tags.notes: Structured programming is programming with sequence, selection, and loops.

rows.title: Introduction to Computer Systems
rows.description: Assembly language programming. Organization of the hardware including registers, memory, and microprocessors and I/O ports. Binary and hexadecimal arithmetic, assembler instructions, processor status (flags), program control, addressing modes.

rows.title: Python Programming
rows.description:
This is a course in which students will learn to program using the Python programming language. Students will also learn the use of Python language and some existing Libraries for performing some AI related tasks.
Sophomore standing or higher is required. Students must be active participants in an EECS program to enroll in this course.

rows.title: Data Structures
rows.description: 1. Pointers and dynamic memory management with objects. 2. Designing of abstract data types, OO programming, and implementing ADTs. 3. Use of templates/generics and STL for container classes 4. Introduction to complexity analysis. Big O notation, asymptotic behavior. 5. Linked-lists: Use them to implement stacks and queues. 6. Implementation as ADTs using templates: Vectors, Lists, Stacks, Queues, Sets,
rows.notes: UC's catalog description may be cut off (ends without punctuation).

rows.title: Information Security and Assurance
rows.description: An introduction to the various technical and administrative aspects of information security and assurance. This course provides the foundation for understanding the key issues associated with protecting information assets, determining the levels of protection and response to security incidents, and designing a consistent, reasonable information security system, with appropriate intrusion detection and reporting features.

rows.title: Discrete Computational Structures
rows.description: Three undergraduate credits. Introduces discrete mathematical topics in the context of CS: mathematical induction, sets, propositional logic, relations and functions, algorithm analysis, graph theory.

rows.title: Programming Languages
rows.description: Concepts and features in design, compilation, and implementation of modern programming languages. Introduction to functional and logic-programming.

rows.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
rows.description: An introduction to the study of sequential algorithms. Analysis of computing time, asymptotic notation, introduction to lower bound theory. Induction, correctness proofs, and recurrence relations. Major design strategies: the greedy method, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming. Graph and network algorithms.

rows.title: Database Design and Development
rows.description: Database design with the Entity Relationship model. Relational data model and database design. Physical storage techniques. Reliability and recovery. Concurrency.

rows.title: Software Engineering
rows.description: Introduction to software engineering and formal methods. General course topics include software lifecycle models, requirements analysis, specification, design, testing and maintenance. The course introduces students to formal methods, global software engineering, and ethics for software engineering. In the lab sessions, students apply concepts taught in lecture, and develop a large group project.

rows.title: Artificial Intelligence: Principles and Applications
rows.description:
1. Fundamental Issues in Intelligent Systems
a. Describe Turing test and Chinese Room Thought Experiment
b. Definitions of AI; Difference between optimum reasoning/behavior and human-like behavior/reasoning
2. Basic Search Strategies
a. Formulate efficient problem/search spaces for a number of problems
b. Combinatorial explosion of search spaces in most problems of interest
c. Usefulness of heuristics, completeness, optimality, time/space complexity during search
d. Uninformed search algorithms
e. Informed Search Algorithms, admissibility, monotonicity, Design a solution using A* search
f. Constraint satisfaction problems, algorithms for their solution
g. Game playing and game tree search, minimax, alpha-beta search
h. Examples of applications of search-based solutions for business and scientific decision making
3. Basic Knowledge Representation
a. Introduction to First Order Predicate Calculus (FOPC)
b. Representation of simple English sentences in FOPC
c. Convert FOPC formulas into clauses
d. Inference rules for FOPC, Resolution, Resolution-refutation, answer-extraction
e. Illustration of modern AI systems such as Watson that represent large volumes of knowledge and their applications in medicine and business
4. Reasoning with uncertainty
a. Probabilistic reasoning
b. Bayes theorem
5. Basic Machine Learning
a. Differences between supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning
b. Examples of data-driven decision support systems for use in business, engineering and sciences

rows.title: Operating Systems and Systems Programming
rows.description: Introduction to concepts of modern operating systems and systems programming. Emphasis is on the concepts, algorithms and architectures of modern operating systems. Students will also learn Unix system programming such as synchronizing, inter-process communication, and networking.

rows.title: Computer Networks and Networked Computing
rows.description: Introduction to basic concepts of computer networks, communication protocols, and computing principles for networked systems.

rows.title: Computer Science Senior Design I
rows.description: First of two semester laboratory series in which students create a significant product capitalizing on their prior four years of computer science education. Each student selects a project advisor, and works with him/her to select a design problem, identify the requirements and specifications of the product, and design the product. Team projects are strongly encouraged.

tags.evidence: identify the requirements and specifications of the product

tags.notes: Team projects are "strongly encouraged", not required.

rows.title: The Theory of Formal Languages and Automata
rows.description: Finite state automata. Regular languages and grammars. Context-free grammars and their normal forms. Pushdown automata. Turing machines. Nondeterministic Turing machines. Universal Turing Machines. The Chomsky hierarchy. The limits of computation. Complexity theory. Finite-state transducers. Moore machines and Mealy machines.

rows.title: Computer Science Senior Design II
rows.description: Second of two semester laboratory series in which students create a significant product capitalizing on their prior four years of computer science education. Completion of detailed design and implementation of project.

rows.title: Introduction to Computer Programming in Java
rows.description: Introduction to computer programming and to problem solving techniques using computer programs; programming lab experience.
rows.notes: Not part of the 126-hour requirements: students take it unless they place out of it (CSE 2221's prerequisite), so counts_toward_total = false.

rows.title: Software I: Software Components
rows.description: Intellectual foundations of software engineering; design-by-contract principles; mathematical modeling of software functionality; component-based software from client perspective; layered data representation.

tags.notes: OSU's layered representation of components (abstraction over an implementation), not bits.

rows.title: Software II: Software Development and Design
rows.description: Data representation using hashing, search trees, and linked data structures; algorithms for sorting; using trees for language processing; component interface design; best practices in Java.

rows.title: Foundations I: Discrete Structures
rows.description: Propositional and first-order logic; basic proof techniques; graphs, trees; analysis of algorithms; asymptotic analysis; recurrence relations.

rows.title: Foundations II: Data Structures and Algorithms
rows.description: Design/analysis of algorithms and data structures; divide-and-conquer; sorting and selection, search trees, hashing, graph algorithms, string matching; probabilistic analysis; randomized algorithms; NP-completeness.

rows.title: Systems I: Introduction to Low-Level Programming and Computer Organization
rows.description: Introduction to computer architecture at machine and assembly language level; pointers and addressing; C programming at machine level; computer organization.

rows.title: Systems II: Introduction to Operating Systems
rows.description: Introduction to operating system concepts: process, CPU scheduling, memory management, file system and storage, and multi-threaded programming.

rows.title: Social, Ethical, and Professional Issues in Computing
rows.description: Social, ethical, and professional issues facing computing professionals; ethical principles; discussion of case studies.
rows.notes: Ethics requirement: the sheet allows CSE 2501 (1 hr) plus a separate 4-hour GE Theme, or PHILOS 2338 (4 hr), which also counts as the Citizenship Theme, plus a 1-hour free elective. The CSE 2501 path is used here (decided with the user).

rows.title: Principles of Programming Languages
rows.description: Formal languages and grammars; recursive descent parsing; data types, expressions, control structures, parameter passing; compilers and interpreters; memory management; functional programming principles.

tags.notes: Data types as a language feature.

rows.title: Program Design II
rows.description: Data abstraction and modular design; recursion; lists and stacks; dynamic memory allocation; file manipulation; programming exercises.

rows.title: Mathematical Foundations of Computing
rows.description: Discrete mathematics concepts fundamental to computing: propositional logic, predicates and quantifiers; proofs; sets; recursive definitions and induction; functions, relations and graphs; combinatorics and discrete probability; applications.

rows.title: Programming Practicum
rows.description: Software development tools and practices; debugging and testing; advanced language features; standard libraries; code management.

rows.title: Data Structures
rows.description: Design, usage and analysis of data structures: review of lists, stacks and queues; hash tables, priority queues, search trees, introduction to graphs; searching and sorting; runtime analysis; programming projects and lab exercises.

rows.title: Machine Organization
rows.description: Data representation and computer arithmetic; machine language; addressing; memory hierarchy; subroutines; data structures; processor architecture: hardware components, pipelining.

tags.notes: Subroutines at the machine level (calls and the stack).

rows.title: Languages and Automata
rows.description: Regular sets and finite automata. Context-free languages and push-down automata. Parsing. Computability theory including Turing machines and decidability.

rows.title: Systems Programming
rows.description: Study of computer systems emphasizing impact on application level programming. Virtual memory and memory management; code optimization; system-level I/O; concurrency: processes, threads, synchronization; introduction to network programming.

tags.notes: Unix-level I/O, as for VT CS 3214 and Purdue CS 24000.

rows.title: Computer Design
rows.description: Computer hardware building blocks. logic gates; combinational circuits; arithmetic circuits; flip flops and sequential circuits; registers and memory; CPU design; I/O design.

rows.title: Software Design
rows.description: Software design principles and practices: Object-oriented design; design patterns; software reuse; testing; event driven programming and concurrency; graphical user interface design and development; Team development.

The automata theory portion includes finite automata, regular expressions, nondeterminism, nonregular languages, context-free languages, pushdown automata, and noncontext-free languages. The computability portion includes Turing machines, the Church-Turing thesis, decidable languages, and the Halting theorem. The complexity portion includes big-O and small-o notation, the classes P and NP, the P vs. NP question, and NP-completeness.

rows.title: The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs

Techniques include procedural abstraction; control abstraction using recursion, higher-order functions, generators, and streams; data abstraction using interfaces, objects, classes, and generic operators; and language abstraction using interpreters and macros. The course exposes students to programming paradigms, including functional, object-oriented, and declarative approaches. It includes an introduction to asymptotic analysis of algorithms. There are several significant programming projects.

We will also target numerous deployment scenarios, including standalone programs, shell scripts, and web-based applications. This course assumes no prior programming experience. rows.title: Principles of Functional Programming
rows.description: An introduction to programming based on a "functional" model of computation. The functional model is a natural generalization of algebra in which programs are formulas that describe the output of a computation in terms of its inputs and #8212;-that is, as a function. But instead of being confined to real- or complex-valued functions, the functional model extends the algebraic view to a very rich class of data types, including not only aggregates built up from other types, but also functions themselves as values. This course is an introduction to programming that is focused on the central concepts of function and type. One major theme is the interplay between inductive types, which are built up incrementally; recursive functions, which compute over inductive types by decomposition; and proof by structural induction, which is used to prove the correctness and time complexity of a recursive function. Another major theme is the role of types in structuring large programs into separate modules, and the integration of imperative programming through the introduction of data types whose values may be altered during computation. NOTE: students must achieve a C or better in order to use this course to satisfy the pre-requisite for any subsequent Computer Science course.

rows.title: Parallel and Sequential Data Structures and Algorithms
rows.description: Teaches students about how to design, analyze, and program algorithms and data structures. The course emphasizes parallel algorithms and analysis, and how sequential algorithms can be considered a special case. The course goes into more theoretical content on algorithm analysis than 15-122 and 15-150 while still including a significant programming component and covering a variety of practical applications such as problems in data analysis, graphics, text processing, and the computational sciences. NOTE: students must achieve a C or better in order to use this course to satisfy the per-requisite for any subsequent Computer Science course.
rows.notes: 12 CMU units.

rows.title: Great Ideas in Theoretical Computer Science
rows.description: This course is about how to use theoretical ideas to formulate and solve problems in computer science. It integrates mathematical material with general problem solving techniques and computer science applications. Examples are drawn from algorithms, complexity theory, game theory, probability theory, graph theory, automata theory, algebra, cryptography, and combinatorics. Assignments involve both mathematical proofs and programming. NOTE: students must achieve a C or better in order to use this course to satisfy the pre-requisite for any subsequent Computer Science course.
rows.notes: 12 CMU units.

rows.title: Algorithm Design and Analysis
rows.description: This course is about the design and analysis of algorithms. We study specific algorithms for a variety of problems, as well as general design and analysis techniques. Specific topics include searching, sorting, algorithms for graph problems, efficient data structures, lower bounds and NP-completeness. A variety of other topics may be covered at the discretion of the instructor. These include parallel algorithms, randomized algorithms, geometric algorithms, low level techniques for efficient programming, cryptography, and cryptographic protocols.
rows.notes: 12 CMU units.

rows.title: Introduction to Computing
rows.description: Introduction to computing principles and programming practices with an emphasis on the design, construction and implementation of problem solutions use of software tools.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 1301 (Thread Hours)'. Counted as Thread Hours on the sheet.

rows.title: Pathways in Computing
rows.description: Small group discussions with first year students are led by one or more faculty members and include a variety of foundational, motivational, and topical subjects for computationalist.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 1100 Freshman Leap'. The 2025-26 sheet calls it 'Freshman Leap'; the 2026-27 catalog title is 'Pathways in Computing'.

rows.title: Introduction to Object Oriented Programming
rows.description: Introduction to techniques and methods of object-oriented programming such an encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism. Emphasis on software development and individual programming skills.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 1331 (Thread Hours)'. Counted as Thread Hours on the sheet.

rows.title: Data Structures and Algorithms for Applications
rows.description: Computer data structures and algorithms in the context of object-oriented programming. Focus on software development towards applications.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 1332 (Thread Hours)'. Counted as Thread Hours on the sheet.

rows.title: Computer Organization and Programming
rows.description: An introduction to basic computer hardware, machine language, assembly language, and C programming.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 2110 (Thread Hours)'. Counted as Thread Hours on the sheet.

rows.title: Objects and Design
rows.description: Object-oriented programming methods for dealing with large programs. Focus on quality processes, effective debugging techniques, and testing to assure a quality product.
rows.notes: Sheet: 'CS 2340 (Thread Hours)'. Counted as Thread Hours on the sheet.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Introduction to Software Design
rows.description: Fundamental concepts of programming from an object-oriented perspective. Basic software engineering principles and programming skills in a programming language that supports the object-oriented paradigm. Simple data types, control structures, array and string data structures, basic algorithms, testing and debugging. A basic model of the computer as an abstract machine. Modeling and problem-solving skills applicable to programming at this level. Partially duplicates 1054, 1124, and 1705.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Software Design and Data Structures
rows.description: A programming-intensive exploration of software design concepts and implementation techniques. Builds on knowledge of fundamental object-oriented programming. Advanced object-oriented software design, ethics in computing, algorithm development and analysis, and classic data structures. Includes a team-based software project.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Computer Science First Year Seminar
rows.description: An introduction to academic and career planning for computer science majors.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Introduction to Problem Solving in Computer Science
rows.description: This course introduces the student to a broad range of heuristics for solving problems in a range of settings that are relevant to computation. Emphasis on problem-solving techniques that aid programmers and computer scientists. Heuristics for solving problems in the small (classical math and word problems), generating potential solutions to real-life problems encountered in the profession, problem solving through computation, and problem solving in teams.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Introduction to Computer Organization
rows.description: An introduction to the design and operation of digital computers. Works up from the logic gate level to combinational and sequential circuits, information representation, computer arithmetic, arithmetic/logic units, control unit design, basic computer organization, relationships between high level programming languages and instruction set architectures. A grade of C or better is required in CS prerequisite. Corequisites: MATH 2534 or MATH 3034.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Introduction to Computer Organization
rows.description: An introduction to the design and operation of digital computers. Instruction formats and construction, addressing modes, instruction execution, memory hierarchy operation and performance, pipelining, input/output, and the relationships between high level programming languages and machine language. A grade of C or better is required in CS pre-requisite 2505 and 2114.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
rows.description: Advanced data structures and analysis of data structure and algorithm performance. Sorting, searching, hashing, and advanced tree structures and algorithms. File system organization and access methods. Ethical issues in the context of data analysis and software performance. Course projects require advanced problem-solving, design, and implementation skills.

File system organization and access methods

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Computer Systems
rows.description: Introduction to computer systems as they are relevant to application programmers today, with emphasis on operating system principles. Operating system design and architectures; processes; threads, synchronization techniques, deadlock; CPU scheduling; system call interfaces, system level I/O and file management; shell programming; separate compilation, loading and linking; inter-process communication (IPC); virtual and physical memory management and garbage collection; network protocols and programming; virtualization; performance analysis and optimization. A grade of C or better is required in CS pre-requisites 2506 and 2114.

tags.notes: Unix-level I/O, as for UIC CS 361.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Professionalism in Computing
rows.description: Studies the ethical, social, and professional concerns of the computer science field. Covers the social impact of the computer, implications and effects of computers on society, and the responsibilities of computer professionals in directing the emerging technology. The topics are studied through case studies of reliable, risk-free technologies, and systems that provide user friendly processes. Specific studies are augmented by an overview of the history of computing, interaction with industrial partners and computing professionals, and attention to the legal and ethical responsibilities of professionals. This is a web-supported course, incorporating writing intensive exercises, making extensive use of active learning technologies. A grade of C or better required in CS prerequisite 3114.

rows.institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
rows.title: Comparative Languages
rows.description: This course in programming language constructs emphasizes the run-time behavior of programs. The languages are studied from two points of view: (1) the fundamental elements of languages and their inclusion in commercially available systems; and (2) the differences between implementations of common elements in languages. A grade of C or better required in CS prerequisite 3114.

rows.title: Computing and Society
rows.description: In this course, students will explore the ways in which computers and information technology shape our lives and society. The course includes a concise introduction to ethics, computing history, and the evolution of the Internet. Students will acquire introductory knowledge in numerous areas where computers and information technology leave a significant impact on society, including privacy, security, freedom of speech, social media, intellectual property, digital citizenship, ethical dilemmas in technology, the environment, and sustainable development. Through the analysis of case studies and real-life scenarios, students will be exposed to ongoing debates surrounding the social, ethical, legal, and policy aspects of computing. This exposure aims to cultivate a critical understanding of how computers influence our society, fostering digital literacy and promoting responsible technology use.

rows.title: Object Oriented Programming with Web-Based Applications
rows.description: The course covers advanced object-oriented principles and their application to web-based, net-centric computing. Major topics include virtual machines, intermediate code generation (Java-specific), graphical user interfaces (GUI) design, event handling, server-side programming with database queries, and security, permissions and file management concepts for client/server systems. Extensive programming assignments provide an understanding of the entire process of client/server development including interface prototyping, program design, implementation of both client and server programs, unit testing, and documentation. This course prepares students to meet immediate demands in solving complex computational problems.

rows.title: Advanced Data Structures and Algorithms in C
rows.description: This course provides a practical introduction to the design, implementation and analysis of advanced data structures and algorithms, using the C programming language and its related command line tools. Data structures include D-ary, Binomial and Fibonacci heaps; Red-Black, splay and quad-trees, along with algorithms for managing and manipulating them. Also covered is the implementation of graph data structures using adjacency lists and adjacency matrices. Graph algorithms studied include searching and minimum spanning tree construction. Pattern matching algorithms include Brute force, Boyer-Moore, KMP, and Rabin-Karp.

rows.title: Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science
rows.description: Discrete mathematics and foundations for modern computer science. Topics include sets, relations, logic, algorithms, graphs, finite state machines and regular expressions.

tags.notes: "logic" alone; not said to be propositional.

rows.title: Computer Systems I
rows.description: This is the first of a two-course sequence to learn the foundations of the underlying hardware and systems software that enable programs to run on a computing platform. This first course covers the architectural issues in the design of modern processor hardware and the operating system software to manage this hardware. On the hardware side, this course covers processor Datapath design, pipelining, instruction scheduling and out-of-order execution, and dealing with branches, interrupts and hazards. Students will also learn about the importance of supporting protection modes in hardware. On the software side, coverage will include instruction set architectures, function calls and interrupt subroutine implementations, translation of C code to assembly, loaders/linkers, address space concepts, processes, threads, context switching and CPU scheduling. At the end, students will understand how to virtualize the processor hardware amongst co-existing activities, ensuring protection and isolation during their execution.

tags.evidence: translation of C code to assembly

rows.title: Software Engineering Principles
rows.description: This course is an introduction to software engineering concepts and principles, project management, and problem-solving for computer science. In this course, students will navigate the entire software development lifecycle and will be familiarized with: problem-solving methodologies for computer science; requirement engineering; project management for CS projects; risk management; software engineering processes; tools and methods for analysis and design of software; methods for testing and evaluating software; quality assurance; ethical and security issues in software engineering. This course gives the student the knowledge and skills needed to successfully develop non-trivial software systems, exploring also social and ethical issues pertinent to software engineering, including privacy, security, intellectual property, responsibility, and social justice.

rows.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
rows.description: Fundamental concepts of computer science: data structures, analysis of algorithms, recursion, trees, sets, graphs, sorting.

rows.title: Computer Systems II
rows.description: This is the second of the two course sequence to learn the foundations of the underlying hardware and systems software that enable programs to run on a computing platform. This course covers the hardware issues in the design of modern memory systems and I/O peripherals and the operating system software to manage such hardware. On the hardware side, this course covers cache design, main memory design, address translation hardware, atomic instructions, buses and interconnects, storage and network peripherals. On the software side, coverage will include concurrency control issues, memory allocation, virtual memory, file systems, device drivers, network programming, distributed systems and protection/isolation. For each hardware resource, students will learn hardware support for protection and software mechanisms to interface with and multiplex this hardware amongst co-existing entities, ensuring appropriate isolation and protection, with appropriate access control mechanisms.

rows.title: Programming Language Concepts
rows.description: Fundamental concepts of programming language design, specifications, and implementation; programming language paradigms and features; program verification.

rows.title: Software Design Methods
rows.description: Applications of scientific knowledge and methods in the design and construction of computer software using engineering concepts.

rows.title: Problem Solving And Object-Oriented Programming
rows.description: Problem solving and algorithms, implementation of algorithms in a high level programming language, conditionals, the iterative approach and debugging, collections of data, searching and sorting, solving problems by decomposition, the object-oriented approach, subclasses of existing classes, handling exceptions that occur when the program is running, graphical user interfaces (GUIs), data stored in files, abstract data types, a glimpse at topics from other CS courses. Intended primarily for students majoring in computer sciences. Credit cannot be obtained for both CS 18000 and any of 15600, 15800 and 15900. Not open to students with credit in CS 24000.
rows.notes: Critical course (Purdue: one a student must pass to persist in the major). Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.

rows.title: Foundations Of Computer Science
rows.description: Logic and proofs; sets, functions, relations, sequences and summations; number representations; counting; fundamentals of the analysis of algorithms; graphs and trees; proof techniques; recursion; Boolean logic; finite state machines; pushdown automata; computability and undecidability.
rows.notes: Critical course (Purdue: one a student must pass to persist in the major). Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.

rows.title: Programming In C
rows.description: The UNIX environment, C development cycle, data representation, operators, program structure, recursion, macros, C preprocessor, pointers and addresses, dynamic memory allocation, structures, unions, typedef, bit-fields, pointer/structure applications, UNIX file abstraction, file access, low-level I/O, concurrency.
rows.notes: Critical course (Purdue: one a student must pass to persist in the major). Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.

rows.title: Computer Architecture
rows.description: Digital logic: transistors, gates, and combinatorial circuits; clocks; registers and register banks; arithmetic-logic units; data representation: big-endian and little-endian integers; ones and twos complement arithmetic; signed and unsigned values; Von-Neumann architecture and bottleneck; instruction sets; RISC and CISC designs; instruction pipelines and stalls; rearranging code; memory and address spaces; physical and virtual memory; interleaving; page tables; memory caches; bus architecture; polling and interrupts; DMA; device programming; assembly language; optimizations; parallelism; data pipelining.
rows.notes: Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.

rows.title: Data Structures And Algorithms
rows.description: Running time analysis of algorithms and their implementations, one-dimensional data structures, trees, heaps, additional sorting algorithms, binary search trees, hash tables, graphs, directed graphs, weighted graph algorithms, additional topics.
rows.notes: Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.

rows.title: Systems Programming
rows.description: Low-level programming; review of addresses, pointers, memory layout, and data representation; text, data, and bss segments; debugging and hex dumps; concurrent execution with threads and processes; address spaces; file names; descriptors and file pointers; inheritance; system calls and library functions; standard I/O and string libraries; simplified socket programming; building tools to help programmers; make and make files; shell scripts and quoting; Unix tools including sed, echo, test, and find; scripting languages such as awk; version control; object and executable files (.o and a.out); symbol tables; pointers to functions; hierarchical directories; and DNS hierarchy; programming embedded systems.
rows.notes: Purdue (Concentration Notes): all major required and track courses need a C or better.
